audience.to: Seven real churches in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea (1:11). They were small groups of Jewish and Gentile believers meeting in homes in busy, proud cities that honored Rome and the emperor with temples, festivals and statues. John, a prophet they knew, wrote from Patmos, where most think he had been exiled "because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus" (1:9). The book was meant to be read aloud in their gatherings (1:3). Their situations differed. Smyrna was poor, slandered and about to face prison. Philadelphia had little strength and faced the same slander. Pergamum had already lost a martyr, Antipas. Thyatira and Pergamum had teachers who said it was fine to eat at idol feasts. Sardis and Laodicea were comfortable and asleep. Each city's history and trade shows through its letter (chapters 2–3).
audience.why: To show these churches who really rules the world, so they would stay faithful to Jesus whatever it cost. For the pressured churches, the visions are comfort: the slaughtered Lamb has already won, God sees the martyrs, and Babylon will fall. For the comfortable churches, they are a warning. In these cities, many trade and social clubs held meals in honor of a god and the emperor. A Christian who stayed away could lose friends, business and standing. Some Christians ("Jezebel," the Nicolaitans) taught that this kind of compromise was harmless. John answers by showing Rome as a beast and a prostitute drunk on the blood of God's people, and by calling, "Come out of her, my people" (18:4). Knowing the first readers changes the reading. The book is not a puzzle about distant dates written over their heads. It is a pastoral letter that uses the pictures of the prophets to tell seven churches what their own choices meant. However a reader applies it today, it first had to make sense in Ephesus and Laodicea.
views: Some scholars (Ramsay, Hemer) think guild life made refusing very costly, so that a Christian worker had to choose between faith and a living. Others (Harland) think joining a club was voluntary, that many Jews and Christians took part in civic life without trouble, and that John was taking a strict line against Christians who saw no harm in it.

Most scholars follow Irenaeus (about 180), who says John saw the vision near the end of Domitian's reign. The churches' settled state (Ephesus has lost its first love, Laodicea is rich after its rebuilding), the spread of emperor worship in Asia, and the name "Babylon" for Rome, which Jewish writers used after Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70, fit this date. So does Polycarp's remark (To the Philippians 11.3) that suggests the church at Smyrna did not yet exist in Paul's day. Some add that the pressure under Domitian came more from local zeal for the emperor than from an empire-wide persecution.

Some scholars date it between 64 and 69, after Nero's killing of Christians in Rome and before the Temple fell. They read the temple that John measures (11:1–2) as still standing, and count the "seven kings" of 17:10 from Julius Caesar or Augustus to land on Nero or Galba. They also argue that Irenaeus's words "it was seen" may refer to John himself, not the vision. Many note that the letters of the name Nero Caesar in Hebrew add up to 666, but many late-date scholars (Bauckham, Aune) accept that too, reading it through the legend that Nero would return, so it is an argument about the beast more than about the date. A few propose the reign of Vespasian (69–79). This date matters most for the Preterist lens, which reads much of the book as fulfilled in the war of AD 66–70.
The first readers were warned about events they would live through: the fall of Jerusalem and the conflict with pagan Rome. The book was mainly for them.
The first readers received the opening of a map of church history that would run from their day to the end. The letters may also stand for ages of the church.

The seven letters were for the first churches (and, for many, for every church), but most of chapters 4–22 describes the last days still to come. The first readers were comforted by knowing how history ends.
The first readers were shown the pattern of every age: the church under pressure from empire and money, and the victory of the Lamb. Their Rome is one face of a power that returns again and again.
Early writers (Tertullian, Clement, Eusebius) say John was exiled there, and most scholars agree. The text says only that he was there "because of the word of God," and a few think he went to preach.

1.what: The title and the first blessing
1.to: the one who reads the book aloud in the churches, and those who hear it
1.when: at the very start, before the letter's greeting
1.why: The book calls itself an unveiling given "to show his servants what must happen soon." Its first blessing is for the reader and the listeners in a gathered church, so the book was made to be heard together, not studied alone. It is the first of seven blessings in Revelation (1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7, 22:14), each a word spoken straight to the hearers.

1.what: The letter's greeting and opening praise
1.to: the seven churches in the province of Asia, gathered to hear the book read aloud
1.when: at the start, in the form of a letter like Paul's
1.why: Revelation begins as a real letter, so everything after it is addressed to these churches. The greeting names God "the one who is, who was, and who is coming," and calls Jesus "the ruler of the kings of the earth": a bold title in cities where the emperor was hailed as lord. The praise reminds small and pressured groups that they are already "a kingdom and priests."

1.by: John, describing the risen Jesus who speaks to him
1.to: the seven churches, who share "the suffering, the kingdom, and the patient endurance" with John
1.when: on the Lord's day, while John was on Patmos, most think as an exile
1.why: The vision shows Jesus walking among the seven lampstands, the churches. Before any warning, the readers learn that he is present with them and holds their "angels" in his hand. His words "Don't be afraid" are for John and also for churches that feared prison and death. Each letter that follows begins with a piece of this picture.

2.when: written to the largest city of Asia, a port and a center of the cult of Artemis, with a temple to the emperors (dedicated about AD 89, so this fits the later date)
2.why: Ephesus was proud, busy and full of religious rivals. The church there had stood firm against false apostles and the Nicolaitans for a long time, but in guarding the truth it had lost the love it had at first. Jesus warns that a church can be right and still lose its place. The promise of "the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" may answer the sacred grove and tree imagery of Artemis's temple.
views: Some read the "love you had at first" as love for Christ, others as love for one another, others as both.

2.when: written to a loyal ally of Rome, among the first cities in Asia to build a temple to Rome, where Christians were poor and faced arrest
2.why: The church in Smyrna gets only praise and comfort. It was poor, perhaps because believers would not join the guilds and festivals, and it was slandered by local opponents John calls "a synagogue of Satan." Accused Christians could be reported to Roman officials. Jesus promises that the suffering will be short ("ten days") and that the faithful will receive "the crown of life." Smyrna's own fame for its "crown" of buildings on the hill may lie behind the image. Polycarp, its bishop, was burned there about 155.
views: Many think they were members of the city's synagogue who opposed the believers, perhaps reporting them to the authorities. John, himself a Jew, denies them the name "Jews." Hemer suggests that after the Jewish tax of Domitian's time, Christians who did not belong to the synagogue were left exposed. Others (Frankfurter, Marshall) think the words come from a dispute inside the Jewish world over who keeps Israel's name, or point at Gentile Christians who claimed to be Jews.

These are harsh words in a quarrel between neighbors, written by a Jew about a local group in one city. They are not a verdict on Jewish people in general, and Christians have done great harm by reading them that way.

2.when: written to the old royal capital, with a great altar of Zeus, the healing shrine of Asclepius (whose sign was a serpent) and the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Rome
2.why: "Where Satan's throne is" fits a city so full of pagan worship and Roman power. The church had held firm when Antipas was killed, but some members followed "the teaching of Balaam," eating idol food and committing sexual sin, which likely meant joining the feasts of temples and trade groups. Jesus calls them to turn back. The promise of "hidden manna" answers their hunger at feasts they had refused; the meaning of the "white stone" is one of many guesses.
views: Readers point to the altar of Zeus, the shrine of Asclepius, or the emperor's temple and the place where the Roman governor held court on his circuit. Several may be meant at once.
Hemer lists many proposals: a vote of acquittal, a token that admitted a guest to a feast, an amulet carrying a secret name, or a jewel like those of the high priest.

2.when: written to a smaller city known for its many trade guilds (dyers, bronze workers, wool and leather workers), whose guardian god, Tyrimnos, was joined with Apollo, a son of Zeus
2.why: Thyatira's church was growing in love and service, but it tolerated a woman prophet John calls "Jezebel" who taught that eating idol food was allowed. For a worker in Thyatira, guild life often included meals in honor of the guild's gods, and her teaching made taking part easy. Jesus, "the Son of God" with feet "like polished bronze," may answer the local son of Zeus and the bronze trade. The promise of authority over the nations is for those who refuse the compromise.
views: Most read the name as a label for a real prophet in the church, taken from the queen in 1 Kings who led Israel to worship Baal. A few see a group, not one woman.
Hemer and Ramsay think guild membership was close to necessary for trade in Thyatira. Harland thinks it was voluntary, and that John is taking a strict side in a debate among Christians.

3.when: written to a once great city, the capital of the old kingdom of Lydia, which twice fell because its watchmen did not keep guard
3.why: Sardis had a name for being alive but was dead. Nothing in the letter speaks of persecution or false teaching; the church was simply at ease with its city. The warning, "Wake up!" and "I will come like a thief," would sting in a city famous for being taken by surprise. A few have kept their clothes clean, a fitting image in a city known for its wool and dye trade.

3.when: written to a small city often shaken by earthquakes, rebuilt with imperial money and once renamed for an emperor
3.why: Like Smyrna, Philadelphia gets no rebuke. It had little strength and was opposed by "the synagogue of Satan," which may mean the believers had been shut out of the synagogue. The promise that these opponents will "come and bow down at your feet" turns around Isaiah 60:14, where the nations bow to Israel: a pointed claim that the promises to Israel belong to this little church too. Jesus, who holds "the key of David," gives them an open door that no one can shut. To people in a city where earthquakes drove residents out to the fields, he promises a place as a pillar in God's temple that "will never leave it again," and a new name, as their city once took a new name from an emperor.
views: Many think they were members of the local synagogue who opposed or expelled the believers. John, himself a Jew, denies them the name. Others (Frankfurter, Marshall) read a dispute within the Jewish world over who is truly Israel, or think the words point at Gentile Christians who claimed to be Jews.
The words belong to a local quarrel in one city in the first century. They are not a judgment on Jewish people as a whole, and reading them that way has done great harm.

Futurist readers often take "keep you from the hour of testing" (3:10) as a promise of rescue before a future tribulation. Others read it as a promise of protection through trial, for this church first.

3.when: written to a rich banking city that rebuilt after the earthquake of AD 60 with its own money, known for black wool and, by many accounts, an eye salve, with water piped in from several miles away
3.why: Laodicea's church shared its city's pride: "I am rich... and need nothing." Jesus may answer with the city's own trades: buy true gold, white clothes instead of famous black wool, and salve for blind eyes. The lukewarm water may echo the city's piped water, lukewarm and hard to drink, in contrast to the hot springs of Hierapolis and the cold water of Colossae nearby. Even so, the letter ends with Jesus at the door, asking to share a meal.
views: Many read the image as useless water, not as a scale of zeal: hot water heals and cold water refreshes, but lukewarm does neither. Others read it as zeal versus indifference.

Ramsay and Hemer tie the gold, wool, salve and water to Laodicea's banks, black wool, medical school and aqueduct. Koester argues they are images any reader in the region would know, from dining and trade, and that the local links are weaker than they look.

4.by: the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders
4.to: God on the throne; overheard by John and, through him, by the seven churches
4.when: in John's vision of heaven, after the door is opened
4.why: The first hymns of heaven say who is truly worthy of worship. The elders lay down their crowns, as client kings bowed before the emperor, and they say "You are worthy, our Lord and God," words like the title "Lord and God" that Suetonius says Domitian liked to hear (that echo assumes the later date). For churches pressed to honor Caesar, the songs declare that only the Creator deserves it. The churches probably sang hymns like these in their own worship.
views: A protest against the emperor cult
Many scholars read these hymns as a deliberate answer to the court ceremony and titles of the emperor.
Others stress that the songs come from Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 and Jewish worship, whatever echo of Rome they carry.

5.what: The angel's question and the elder's comfort
5.by: a mighty angel, then one of the elders
5.to: all creation, then John, who is weeping
5.when: when no one is found worthy to open the sealed scroll
5.why: The angel asks "Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?" The elder tells John "Stop crying!" and points to the Lion of Judah. John then sees a slaughtered Lamb. For the churches, the Messiah they hoped for wins not by force but by dying, and that is the pattern for their own victory.

5.what: The new song to the Lamb
5.by: the living creatures and the elders, then many angels, then every creature
5.to: the Lamb who was slaughtered, and God on the throne
5.when: after the Lamb takes the sealed scroll
5.why: The hymn explains why the Lamb can open the scroll: not by force but because he was killed and bought people "from every tribe, language, people, and nation." For small house churches, the song says that they belong to a worldwide kingdom of priests, and that victory comes the way the Lamb won it, by faithful suffering. The circle of praise grows until all creation joins.

6.what: The martyrs' prayer and the answer
6.by: the souls under the altar of those killed for God's word; then a reply from heaven
6.when: when the Lamb breaks the fifth seal
6.why: The martyrs ask "how long" until God judges, a cry from the psalms. They are given white robes and told to rest a little longer, because more will be killed. For churches that knew of Antipas's death and feared more, the answer is honest: suffering is not over yet, but God has heard, and the dead are safe with him. Later scenes (16:5–7, 19:2) answer this prayer.
views: Some readers find the prayer vengeful. Others note that it asks God, not the church, to act, and that it is a plea for justice like those in the psalms.

6.what: The cry of the kings to the mountains
6.by: the kings, rulers, generals, the rich and the powerful, and every slave and free person
6.when: at the opening of the sixth seal, as the sky and earth are shaken
6.why: The powerful people who seemed safe now hide, saying "Fall on us and hide us," words from Hosea. Their question "who can stand?" is answered in chapter 7. For small churches under the rule of the powerful, it shows that no rank protects anyone before God.

7.what: The command to seal God's servants
7.by: an angel with the seal of the living God
7.to: the four angels holding back the winds
7.when: between the sixth and seventh seals
7.why: Before harm comes, God marks his own. The scene draws on Ezekiel 9, where those who grieve over the city's sins are marked before judgment. For the churches, it says God protects his people through the trouble, not that they escape all suffering.

7.what: The praise of the countless crowd, and the elder's answer
7.by: a crowd from every nation, the angels, and one of the elders
7.to: God and the Lamb; the elder speaks to John
7.when: between the sixth and seventh seals, after the sealing of the 144,000
7.why: The vision answers the question at the end of chapter 6, "who can stand?" The crowd in white has "come out of the great suffering." For churches facing poverty and prison, the elder's words promise shelter, no more hunger or thirst, and that "God will wipe every tear from their eyes."
views: Some read the crowd as the martyrs; others as the whole church, or the 144,000 seen from another side.

Preterists link it to the trials of the first century, futurists to a coming tribulation, historicists to the trials of the church through its history, such as the persecutions under the later emperors, and idealists to the suffering of the church in every age.

8.to: "the people who live on the earth"
8.why: The cry warns that the last three trumpets will be worse. In Revelation "the people who live on the earth" usually means those who side with the beast against God's people. For the churches, the warning shows that the trumpets are calls to repent before it is too late (9:20–21).

10.what: The angel's oath and John's new call
10.by: a mighty angel, a voice from heaven, and then a voice telling John to prophesy
10.to: John, and through him the churches
10.when: between the sixth and seventh trumpets
10.why: The angel swears "There will be no more delay!" John eats the little scroll, sweet in his mouth but sour in his stomach, as Ezekiel ate his scroll. Then he is told, "You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings." The second half of the book is framed as a message to the nations, and the bitter taste warns the churches that their witness will cost them.
views: Some take it as the same scroll the Lamb opened in chapter 5 (Bauckham), others as a smaller message, the content of chapter 11 or of chapters 11–22.

11.what: The command to measure the temple
11.when: just after he is told to prophesy again
11.why: John measures the temple, the altar and the worshipers, but leaves out the outer court, given to the nations for 42 months. The measuring marks God's people as protected in their worship even while the city is trampled. Two witnesses are given power to prophesy. For the churches, the scene pictures their role: to witness in a hostile world.
views: Early-date scholars and preterists read this as the Jerusalem temple before AD 70, so it helps date the book.
Most late-date scholars read the temple as God's people, as Paul uses the image in 1 Corinthians 3:16.
Futurists often expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem.
Historicists have read the 42 months as 1,260 years of church history, often of papal power.

11.what: The song at the seventh trumpet
11.by: loud voices in heaven and the twenty-four elders
11.when: when the seventh angel blows his trumpet
11.why: Heaven announces the end before the book has shown it: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ." The churches lived in "the kingdom of the world" ruled by Rome. The song tells them that the change of rule is certain and that God will "reward your servants the prophets, your people, and those who fear your name."

12.what: The victory song after the war in heaven
12.to: the heavens, and a warning to the earth and the sea; heard by John
12.when: after Michael throws the dragon down
12.why: The song explains the churches' suffering. Satan has lost in heaven and rages on earth because "he knows his time is short." The believers defeat him "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony," even if it costs their lives. Persecution is a sign of the dragon's defeat, not of his strength.

13.to: the churches hearing the book read
13.when: after the beast from the sea makes war on God's people
13.why: John uses the same words that end each of the seven letters, so the hearers know this is meant for them. The saying, based on Jeremiah 15:2, tells them not to fight back but to accept prison or death if it comes. "This calls for patient endurance and faithfulness from God's people."
views: Manuscripts differ in 13:10. Some say whoever kills with the sword must be killed with the sword, a warning against taking up arms.

13.what: The mark and the riddle of 666
13.when: after the beast from the earth makes everyone take the mark
13.why: "No one can buy or sell" unless they have the mark. For hearers in trading cities, the picture of the economy bound up with worship of the beast was close to home. John then gives a puzzle meant to be solved: "it is a human number." In the ancient practice of gematria, letters stood for numbers. A few manuscripts read 616, which also fits the name Nero Caesar spelled in Hebrew in its Latin form.
views: Preterists, and many late-date scholars too, read 666 as Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters, perhaps as the Nero expected to return.
Futurists expect a coming Antichrist whose name will fit the number.
Historicists read it as the papacy, often through the Greek word Lateinos (the Latin one), whose letters add up to 666, as Irenaeus already noted.
Idealists read it as the number of imperfection: six, short of seven, three times over.

14.what: The new song before the throne, learned by the 144,000
14.by: a choir in heaven, like harpists (some say the 144,000 themselves)
14.to: sung before the throne, the creatures and the elders; heard by John
14.when: right after the visions of the two beasts and the mark
14.why: In contrast to those who take the beast's mark, the 144,000 carry the Lamb's name. They alone can learn heaven's new song, and they "follow the Lamb wherever he goes." For the churches, the picture shows what faithfulness looks like. Some read the group as an army kept ready for holy war, and their purity as refusing the idolatry Revelation calls sexual sin.
views: Many futurists read them as ethnic Israel or Jewish believers. Bauckham, Beale and others read them as the whole church, pictured as the true Israel. Others read them as the martyrs.
Most read the words about women as a picture of refusing idolatry. Some read a holy-war rule, as soldiers kept apart before battle. A few read literal celibacy.

14.what: The messages of the three angels
14.by: three angels, a voice from heaven and the Spirit
14.to: "those who live on the earth," every nation, and through John the churches
14.when: before the harvest of the earth and the bowls
14.why: The first angel calls all nations to "Fear God and give him glory" and to worship the Creator: a last call to repent. The second announces Babylon's fall ahead of time. The third warns that anyone who worships the beast and takes its mark will share God's anger. For believers tempted to join the club feasts and honor the emperor to keep their business and standing, the warning is meant to make the cost of compromise plain. Then come comfort and a call: "This calls for patient endurance," and a blessing on those who die in the Lord.
views: Preterists and many others link the mark to taking part in emperor worship and the trade and civic life bound up with it. Historicists read it as loyalty to papal Rome. Futurists often expect a future mark. Idealists read it as any loyalty to a power that takes God's place.

15.what: The song of Moses and the Lamb
15.by: those who won the victory over the beast
15.when: beside the sea of glass, before the seven bowls
15.why: As Israel sang beside the sea after the Exodus, the faithful sing after their own rescue. The words come almost entirely from the psalms and prophets. The song does not praise their own victory but God's justice, and it hopes that "All nations will come and worship." Even before the last plagues, the goal is the nations turning to God.

16.what: The angel's praise of God's justice
16.by: the angel in charge of the waters, and the altar
16.when: after the third bowl turns the rivers to blood
16.why: The short song answers the martyrs' cry in 6:10. Those who shed the blood of God's people are given blood to drink. For churches that knew of Antipas's death and feared more deaths, it says God's judgments are true and just.

16.what: Jesus breaks in: "I am coming like a thief"
16.when: in the middle of the sixth bowl, as the kings gather for Armageddon
16.why: Jesus suddenly speaks straight to the hearers with the third of the book's seven blessings. The words echo the letters to Sardis ("I will come like a thief") and Laodicea (white clothes to cover "your shameful nakedness"). Even in the great battle scene, the point for the churches is to stay awake and faithful now.

17.what: The angel explains the woman and the beast
17.by: one of the seven angels with the bowls
17.to: John, and through him the churches
17.when: after John is amazed at the woman on the scarlet beast
17.why: The angel gives clues the first readers could decode: seven mountains (Rome was the city on seven hills), seven kings, and "the great city that rules over the kings of the earth." The aim was to help believers see the empire's glittering capital through heaven's eyes, so that they would not admire it.
views: Most scholars read the woman as Rome and its economy and the kings as emperors, though they count the kings in different ways, which affects the date of the book.
Some preterists read the prostitute as the Jerusalem that rejected Jesus.
Historicists, including the Reformers, read Babylon and the beast as papal Rome.
A future power or every empire
Futurists often expect a revived Rome or a world system to come; idealists see every proud, wealthy power.

18.what: The angel's cry and the call to come out
18.by: an angel with great authority, then another voice from heaven
18.to: the world, and "my people" among the nations
18.when: after the vision of the woman on the beast
18.why: "Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the Great!" echoes Isaiah and Jeremiah on ancient Babylon. The voice from heaven tells God's people to leave her. Most read this as refusing to share her sins and pride. Some read a real flight, as in Jeremiah 51:45, and preterists who see Jerusalem in Babylon link it to the Christians who fled before AD 70. For merchants and workers in Asia whose living was tied to Roman trade, this was a hard and practical call.

18.what: The laments of the kings, merchants and sailors
18.by: the kings of the earth, the merchants, the sea traders, and then a mighty angel
18.to: the fallen city; heard by John and the churches
18.when: as the smoke of Babylon's burning rises
18.why: The mourners stand far away and weep for their lost profit, not for the city. The long cargo list, from gold and silk to "slaves, that is, human lives," lays out the goods that flowed to Rome from across the empire, some through ports like Ephesus and Smyrna. The point for the churches is to see that economy as God sees it: built on luxury and on people bought and sold. The angel's millstone and the silence of music and lamps show it will not be rebuilt. Heaven is told to celebrate, because God has judged her for the way she treated his people.
views: Most scholars read the laments as a picture of the Roman economy in John's day, modeled on Ezekiel 27 on Tyre.

Preterists who see Babylon as Jerusalem read the laments as about the Temple's wealth. Historicists read them as the fall of papal Rome. Futurists expect a coming world economy. Idealists see the fall of every system that treats people as cargo.

19.what: The Hallelujah songs, the wedding of the Lamb, and a blessing
19.by: a huge crowd in heaven, the elders and living creatures, a voice from the throne, and the angel
19.to: God, and the angel speaks to John
19.why: Heaven answers the laments of chapter 18 with joy. The crowd praises God for justice and announces a wedding: the church, dressed in "fine linen, bright and clean," in contrast to the prostitute's purple and gold. For the churches, the contrast is a choice between two cities and two women. The angel adds a blessing, "Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb!" When John falls to worship the angel he is told "Worship God!", a sharp word for readers tempted to honor powers other than God.

19.what: The angel's call to the birds
19.by: an angel standing in the sun
19.to: all the birds flying high overhead
19.when: as the rider on the white horse goes out against the beast
19.why: "The great supper of God" is a grim reverse of the Lamb's wedding supper (19:9), drawn from Ezekiel 39. Those who sided with the beast, from kings to slaves, end as food for birds. For the churches, the two suppers show where each loyalty leads.

20.what: The blessing on the first resurrection
20.to: the churches, and those who stay faithful to death
20.when: after the vision of the martyrs who reign for a thousand years
20.why: The fifth of the book's seven blessings tells hearers who feared death for their faith that the second death has no power over them, and that they will be "priests of God and of Christ." For a church that had lost Antipas, it is a promise that the faithful dead are not losers but rulers.
views: Premillennial readers, most futurists among them, expect a literal thousand-year reign after Christ returns.
Amillennial readers, following Augustine, read the thousand years as the church age now, with the martyrs reigning in heaven.
Some read it as a coming golden age of the gospel before Christ returns. Historicists have often held this or the amillennial view.

21.by: a loud voice from the throne, then God himself
21.to: John and the churches, and "the one who is thirsty"
21.when: as the new Jerusalem comes down out of heaven
21.why: God promises to live with his people, wipe every tear and end death and pain. He offers the water of life as a free gift, and names "the one who wins the victory" as his heir, the same promise made at the end of each of the seven letters. The warning list that follows (the cowardly, the idol worshipers, the liars) reminds the churches that the choices in chapters 2–3 decide who enters.

22.by: the angel, Jesus, the Spirit and the bride, and John
22.to: the seven churches who hear the book read aloud, and everyone who hears it
22.when: at the end of the book, as the letter closes
22.why: The ending returns to the churches and to the urgency of the start: "Look, I am coming soon!" John is told not to seal the book, "because the time is near": it was meant for its first hearers, not to be locked away for a far future. Jesus speaks in his own name: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to give you this testimony for the churches." The invitation to come and drink, the warning not to add to or take from the book, and the prayer "Come, Lord Jesus!" end it as worship, as it would have been heard in the gathering.
views: Preterists read "soon" and "near" as pointing to events in the first readers' lifetime. Historicists read them as the start of a sequence that began in John's day and runs through church history. Futurists read them as the certainty or suddenness of Christ's return. Idealists read them as the nearness of judgment and hope in every age.

traditions.q: Does Revelation fully belong in the Bible, and should it be read in church worship?
views: It is Scripture, but the East accepted it slowly. Dionysius of Alexandria (about 250) doubted that the apostle wrote it, and Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) left it off his list of books; to this day it is never read in the Divine Liturgy. Andrew of Caesarea's commentary (about 611) became the church's standard guide to it.

Coptic and Ethiopian Bibles include it (the Coptic Church reads the whole book aloud through the night of Holy Saturday, called Apocalypse Night), but others came late. The Armenian Church placed it in its canon only in the Middle Ages, around the 1100s, and the old Syriac Bible (the Peshitta) did not have it; the Syriac Orthodox now accept it, while the separate Assyrian Church of the East has traditionally left it out of its canon.

Yes, without doubt. The West received it early, the councils of Hippo and Carthage (393, 397) list it, Trent (1546) names it the Apocalypse of John the apostle, and it is read at Mass on the Sundays of Easter in one year of the cycle and on the feast of the Assumption.

Received, with a famous early doubt. In 1522 Luther wrote that he missed more than one thing in this book and could hold it neither apostolic nor prophetic; by 1530 he read it more warmly as a picture of church history. Lutherans today read Revelation 14:6–7 on Reformation Day, though Chemnitz counted it among the once-disputed books.

Yes, but the early Reformers kept their distance. Zwingli said it was not a biblical book, and Calvin wrote commentaries on every New Testament book except Revelation and 2–3 John. The Westminster Confession lists it with the rest of the canon.

1.q: John was in the Spirit "on the Lord's day" (1:10). Does that mean Sunday, and should Christians keep Sunday instead of the Sabbath?
views: Yes. The Lord's day is Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and from the start Christians gathered on it (the Didache calls it the Lord's own day). Sunday fulfills the Sabbath and takes its place as the day to worship and rest (Catechism 2174–2175).

It means Sunday, but Sunday is not a law. The Augsburg Confession (article 28) says the Sabbath of Moses has ended and the church chose the Lord's day in Christian freedom, as a good order for worship, not as a command that binds the conscience.

It means Sunday, and the Sabbath command still applies to it. The Westminster Confession calls the first day "the Lord's day," citing this verse, and says it is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy until the end of the world.

No. The only day the Bible says the Lord owns is the seventh day, of which Jesus said he is Lord (Mark 2:28), and nothing here says Sunday. Adventists keep the Saturday Sabbath and teach that Sunday worship came in later, mainly through the church at Rome.

2.q: Do the seven churches of chapters 2–3 stand for seven ages of church history?
views: Yes, in part. The Scofield Reference Bible says the letters are real messages to real churches, but also a prophetic outline of church history from the apostles to the end, with lukewarm Laodicea as the church of the last days.

Yes. Traditional Adventist teaching gives each church a period, from Ephesus in the apostles' age to Philadelphia in the revival of the 1840s and Laodicea in the time of the judgment. Adventists have often applied the warning to Laodicea to their own church.

No. They were real churches, and because there are seven, the number of completeness, together they stand for the whole church in every age. Victorinus, writing the oldest surviving Latin commentary (about 260), said that what is said to one church is said to all.

No. Each letter ends by saying what the Spirit says "to the churches," plural, so every letter speaks to every congregation in every age. Reformed scholars find nothing in the text that marks out periods of history.

3.q: "I will also keep you from the hour of testing" (3:10). Will the church be taken up to heaven before the great tribulation?
views: Yes. Jesus will come for his church in a secret rapture before seven years of tribulation, and 3:10 promises to keep believers out of that hour, not safe through it. After chapter 3 the word "church" does not appear again until 22:16, and John's call to "come up here" (4:1) pictures the rapture (Darby, Scofield, Walvoord, Pentecost).
Mostly yes. The Assemblies of God calls the rapture of the church "the blessed hope" and teaches that it is imminent, coming before the tribulation. Some Pentecostal groups hold other timings.

Divided. Many Baptists, especially in America, hold a pre-tribulation rapture, while others, like the Baptist scholar George Eldon Ladd, say Christ returns once, after the tribulation, and that "keep you from" means protecting believers through it, as in Jesus's prayer in John 17:15. The Baptist Faith and Message does not decide.

No separate rapture. Christ will return once, in glory, and before that the church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many (Catechism 675). Being "caught up" (1 Thessalonians 4:17) is the meeting with the Lord at that one coming.

No. Reformed teachers, like Lutherans and the Orthodox, see one visible return of Christ at the end. Believers are kept from God's wrath but not from suffering, which is what the faithful in Revelation endure.

5.q: The elders hold gold bowls full of incense, "which are the prayers of God's people" (5:8; see 6:9–10 and 8:3–4). Do the saints in heaven pray for us, and may we ask them to?
views: Yes. The saints in heaven are alive in Christ, care for those still on earth and pray for them, so it is good to ask their prayers, as you would ask a friend's (Catechism 956, 2683). Scenes like this one show heaven taking part in the prayers of the church.

Yes. Asking the Mother of God and the saints to pray for us belongs to every service, and incense rises in Orthodox worship as it does before the throne here. The church in heaven and on earth is one family at prayer.

The saints do pray for the church, but we should not pray to them. The Augsburg Confession (article 21) says the saints should be remembered as examples of faith, but Scripture does not teach calling on them, since Christ is the one mediator.
Divided. The Thirty-Nine Articles (article 22) reject the invocation of saints, and many Anglicans follow that, while Anglo-Catholics ask the saints' prayers much as Catholics do.

No. The Westminster Confession says prayer is to be made to God alone, not to angels or saints. The bowls hold the prayers of believers on earth, which come before God through Christ, and the scene does not show anyone praying to the elders.

7.q: Who are the 144,000 sealed "from all the tribes of Israel" (7:4; 14:1–5), and how do they relate to the great crowd (7:9)?
views: The number is literal. The 144,000 are anointed Christians chosen since Pentecost who will rule with Christ in heaven, while the great crowd are faithful people who will live forever on a restored earth; only the anointed eat the bread and drink the wine at the yearly Memorial.

They are 12,000 Jews from each tribe of Israel, sealed during the future tribulation after the church has been raptured. Many teachers think they will preach during that time, and the great crowd are people saved through their witness.

Early Adventists linked the 144,000 to the faithful who are alive when Christ returns. Ellen White warned members not to argue about who they will be, and Adventists today hold several views, many taking the number as symbolic.

The number is a symbol: twelve tribes times twelve times a thousand, the complete people of God built on Israel and the apostles. The Catechism counts the 144,000 as the new People of God in heaven's worship, alongside the great crowd from every nation (Catechism 1138). Catholic writers differ on whether the two groups are one, and the Church reads this chapter on All Saints' Day.

The 144,000 and the great crowd are one group. John hears a number and then sees a crowd, just as he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb (5:5–6): the church is the true Israel, counted and complete, yet too many to count.

12.q: Is the woman dressed in the sun, who gives birth to the Messiah (12:1–6), Mary?
views: Yes, and also the people of God. The Church reads 11:19 and 12:1–6 on the feast of the Assumption: the ark of the covenant seen in heaven is followed by the woman, and Mary is the ark who carried Christ. Pius XII noted that teachers of the church saw Mary's glory in this woman (Munificentissimus Deus 27), and the Catechism names Mary as the Woman in heaven's worship (Catechism 1138).

Mainly the church. Andrew of Caesarea, the standard Orthodox commentator, reports that some understand her as the Mother of God but follows Methodius in seeing the church, which always gives birth to Christ in believers. The Marian reading is honored, not required.

The faithful people of God: Israel, from whom the Messiah was born, continuing as the church that the dragon still attacks (12:17). Some Protestants allow that Mary is in the background, as the mother of the child, but not that the chapter teaches about her.

National Israel. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph's dream of his family (Genesis 37:9), and the woman's flight into the wilderness is Israel protected in the last three and a half years of the tribulation.

13.q: Is the beast of chapter 13, or the Antichrist, the papacy?
views: Historically, yes. Luther's Smalcald Articles say the pope is the very Antichrist, and his 1530 preface reads the second beast of chapter 13 as the papacy, which set up a new Roman Empire as the beast's image. The Missouri Synod's Brief Statement (1932) still says this, though many Lutherans, especially those in dialogue with Rome, no longer do.

Historically, yes. The Westminster Confession of 1646 (and the 1689 Baptist confession) called the pope "that Antichrist." Many Presbyterian churches have since removed the line, and most Reformed scholars now read the beast as Rome in John's day and the powers like it.

Yes. Traditional Adventist teaching, following Ellen White, reads the sea beast as papal Rome, the 42 months as 1,260 years (AD 538–1798), and the healing of its wound as the papacy's return to power; the land beast is the United States, which will one day enforce worship on Sunday.

No. The beast is the emperor-worshiping Rome that killed Peter and Paul and the martyrs, and every power that demands worship. The Antichrist is a final religious lie in which people put themselves in the place of God (Catechism 675–676).

No. Following Irenaeus, Hippolytus and Andrew of Caesarea, the Orthodox expect the Antichrist to be a single deceiver near the end of history, and see beasts at work wherever the state claims worship.
No. The beast is a future world ruler at the head of a revived Roman Empire, who makes and then breaks a treaty with Israel (Daniel 9:27) and rules for the last three and a half years.

17.q: Who is Babylon the prostitute (chapters 17–18), and what does "Come out of her, my people" (18:4) ask?
views: Pagan imperial Rome, the city on seven hills that killed the martyrs, which 1 Peter 5:13 already calls Babylon; and every worldly power like it. Some Catholic writers, such as Scott Hahn, read her instead as Jerusalem that had become unfaithful.

The Reformers read Babylon as papal Rome: the Geneva Bible's notes say so plainly. Most Reformed scholars today read first-century Rome and every society that trades with anyone and worships its own wealth.

Babylon is fallen religion: Rome and the churches that keep her teachings, such as Sunday worship. "Come out of her" is God's last call to his true people, many of whom are still in those churches, to leave before the end.

A future false world religion (chapter 17) and a future world economy or city (chapter 18), which some think will be Babylon in Iraq rebuilt. The beast will turn on the religious system before God judges both.

20.q: What are the thousand years (20:1–6), and when are they?
views: The present age of the church, in which Christ already reigns with his saints (Augustine). The Church rejects millenarianism, the hope of an earthly kingdom of Christ within history, even in milder forms (Catechism 676).
The time between Christ's first coming and the end, as Andrew of Caesarea taught. Some early fathers, such as Papias and Irenaeus, expected an earthly reign, but the church did not follow them.
The present reign of Christ. The Augsburg Confession (article 17) rejects the "Jewish opinions" that before the resurrection the godly will take over the kingdoms of the world.

No confession decides, and Reformed churches hold two views. Amillennialists (such as Anthony Hoekema) say it is the present church age; postmillennialists (many Puritans, Jonathan Edwards, B. B. Warfield) expect the gospel to win most of the world before Christ returns.

Divided. Baptists hold every view, and the Baptist Faith and Message (article 10) says only that God will bring the world to its end in his own time and way. Historic premillennialists like Ladd expect Christ to return before an earthly reign.

A literal future thousand years after Christ returns, when he reigns on earth from Jerusalem and God's promises to Israel as a nation are fulfilled. The Assemblies of God and many other Pentecostals hold a similar premillennial view.

Premillennial, but in heaven. At Christ's return the saved are taken to heaven for the thousand years while the earth lies empty and Satan is bound there with no one to tempt; then the holy city comes down, and the wicked are destroyed.
